item.title: Honoring Thy Self: The Unsung Virtues of Selfishness
item.description:
Self-Help

Honoring Thy Self: The Unsung Virtues of Selfishness

Is our society becoming more or less selfish?

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • Selfishness is often demonized in our society.
  • Sometimes the solution to the problems people bring to therapy is being more selfish, not less.
Avarice (Avaritia) from The Deadly Seven Sins (The Met)
Source: Pieter van der Heyden, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Is selfishness ever a virtue? We live in a culture that worships selflessness and despises selfishness. Most of us are taught from a very early age that it is bad or sinful to be selfish. Selfishness is denounced by parents, teachers, friends, etc., and children are frequently punished by scolding, shaming, berating, humiliating, criticizing, and, in some cases, even beating them. Religion, culture, and modern psychology have contributed to this exceedingly negative attitude toward the expression of selfishness, whether in children, adolescents, or adults.

Societally, we seem to believe that selfishness is an evil tendency or trait that must be forcibly exorcised as soon as possible in the service of what we euphemistically call socialization—the massive suppression and denial of our most basic, vital, and essential self. Sigmund Freud, in Civilization and its Discontents (1929), recognized that human beings are naturally and inherently selfish, which can be antithetical to creating community and collective culture, and, therefore, such selfish tendencies, he said, must be suppressed, denied, or repressed.

Yet, despite thousands of years of suppression, pathological or neurotic selfishness, or what we today call narcissism, is even more ubiquitous, pervasive, and problematical than ever. Why? Could we paradoxically be engendering more neurotic or psychotic selfishness in our culture by suppressing and denigrating our innate, normal, or healthy selfishness? Might our entire approach to the problem of selfishness be grossly misguided and ultimately self-defeating?

Clearly, when we are speaking of selfishness as excessive egoism, self-centeredness, greediness, narcissism, cruelty, violence, and being inconsiderate of and insensitive to the needs, dignity, and feelings of others, this is certainly something negative, destructive, evil, and undesirable, though, to some extent, tragically unavoidable in human society. Psychoanalyst Heinz Kohut (1978) theorized that, paradoxically, neurotic or pathological narcissism stems from childhood suppression or negation of our necessary natural or “healthy narcissism.” This is a kind of axiomatic psychological truth: that which we chronically suppress, repress, or deny in ourselves eventually expresses itself in even more negative and destructive ways. Another good example of this is the primitive emotion of anger, which, when chronically repressed, can cause various psychological and somatic symptomatology, including headaches, depression, resentment, embitterment, hostility, rage attacks, aggression, and destructive and violent behavior toward ourselves or others (see Diamond, 1996, 2025).

For Freud (1950), the primordial passions of what he termed the id are defined as any powerful feeling, impulse, or emotion, such as sexuality, aggression, love, or hate, Eros or Thanatos, and are metaphorically described as “a chaos, a cauldron full of seething excitations.” Existential psychoanalyst Rollo May (1969) referred to such primal, natural human emotions, instincts, and proclivities as anger, rage, sex, anxiety, selfishness, and craving power and control collectively as the daimonic, “the urge in every being to affirm itself, assert itself, perpetuate and increase itself.” (See Diamond, 1996, 2025.) When the daimonic is chronically or habitually denied or repressed, it tends to be expressed or manifest negatively and destructively. Why? As Jung indicated in his concept of the shadow, just because we suppress or deny our rage, sexual desires, or selfishness, rendering them unconscious, it does not make such feelings magically disappear; on the contrary, it only amplifies and makes them stronger, more powerful, difficult to manage, and potentially more dangerous and destructive.

This is equally true of so-called selfishness. When denied or suppressed over time, it is reduced to its lowest, most primitive, evil, ugly, dangerous, antisocial, inhumane, and negative form: greed, lust, inflation, grandiosity, authoritarianism, domination, sadism, omnipotence, psychopathy, etc. It can take complete possession of us, body and soul, and compel us to behave badly. This is an expression of the negative, evil, destructive side of selfishness and of the id, daimonic, or shadow in general. But when we can acknowledge, accept, embrace, and assert rather than routinely deny or repress our intrinsic selfishness, it can manifest more constructively, prosocially, and even creatively as we become more authentically true to ourselves.

But there is yet another kind of selfishness, one that centers not solely on the ego but on the needs of what Jung called the self and the individual’s congenital tendency to, as Jungian analyst John Beebe (1996) in his blurb for my book so pithily puts it, outwardly express “this strongly self-assertive energy, so glibly dismissed as narcissism... [Diamond] discloses the daimonic as the self’s essential capacity to claim and defend its own right to being itself.” Indeed, one of the most difficult tasks for some psychotherapy patients is learning to be selfish in the right way. To consciously acknowledge and assert their most fundamental wants and needs, their deepest dreams and desires, their most passionate emotions. It contradicts everything they were ever taught and engenders strong guilt feelings. For them, being selfish is one of the hardest things to do, but it is absolutely essential if they are serious about improving the quality of their lives.

Jung differentiated between what he called the self and the ego, the part of our personality with which we tend to most closely identify and experience as its center. Jung (1961) places the ego and the persona in a subordinate, secondary, and subservient position in relation to the self, which he defines as “the central archetype. . . . the totality of the personality. . . . The self is not only the centre but also the whole circumference which embraces both conscious and unconscious; it is the centre of this totality, just as the ego is the centre of the conscious mind.” When we think about selfishness, this typically has more to do with being oriented toward the wants and needs of the ego rather than of the self. But when we deny or refuse to acknowledge and, when appropriate, obey the desires of the self, which can sometimes be antithetical to or contradict those of the ego, there can be even more tragic consequences.

In the Old Testament, Jonah heard an inner voice, presumably from God, telling him to go to Nineveh, but chose to go instead to the town of Tarshish. From a psychological perspective, was this his ego or the self speaking? I would venture to say the latter, and that his rebellious decision to do what he wanted instead came from his ego.

Each of us has some mysterious inner voice (not a hallucination), daimon, soul, or self urging us toward our destiny that we choose either to listen to, respect, and obey, or ignore, deny, and run from. But, as with Jonah, there is always a heavy price to pay for ignoring or fleeing from one’s self. For refusing or failing to find the requisite courage to selfishly accept and pursue this calling despite what others, society, or sometimes one’s own ego or persona, say.

In this sense, selfishness requires acknowledging, rather than repressing, not only the primitive, animalistic, instinctual desires of the ego but also carefully and courageously listening to, discerning, and pursuing the deeper desires of the self. This is healthy or spiritual selfishness. Becoming more, not less, self-ish: i.e., conscious of and attuned to the deepest and most meaningful needs of the self.

item.title: Keeping Mentally Healthy in Trauma Nursing
item.description:
Trauma

Keeping Mentally Healthy in Trauma Nursing

Emily Ragus discusses her shift from practice in trauma nursing to research.

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • In trauma nursing, mental health is not separated from physical health, for patients and for medical staff.
  • Emily Ragus went from practice to research in order to improve mental health in trauma nursing.
  • Listening to disaster responders describe the mental health impact of their work supports their mental health.

In June 2016, a bus carrying Australian tourists crashed head-on into a local bus in Port Vila, the capital city of the Pacific island country of Vanuatu. Three people in the local bus died. A dozen Australians were hurt, including head injuries and open fractures. As one incident within her 15 years of trauma nursing, Emily Ragus helped evacuate some of them to Australia for medical care through CareFlight.

Emily recounts the epiphany, “The usual fairness issues appeared. Australian tourists received deserved world-class emergency help while the people of Vanuatu struggle with daily health services. But nor should tourists take away valuable healthcare resources from locals, so evacuations can help equity. And part of this balance is mental health connected to physical health, for the responders as well as for the crash-affected people and their families.”

Emily flying with members of the Swedish National Air Medivac (SNAM) during her Churchill Fellowship in Sweden in 2019.
Source: Emily Ragus

This experience led Emily to apply for and win a Winston Churchill Fellowship in 2018 to earn a Diploma of International Humanitarian Assistance from Fordham University in New York City. She formulated ideas about keeping mentally healthy while being a trauma nurse, especially since mental health is not separate from the physical care she provides. Emily’s exploration into these topics led her to win a prestigious Sir John Monash Scholarship for an anthropology Ph.D. at the University of Amsterdam in the Netherlands.

Broad connections with mental health

Emily explains, “I am a listener and teller of stories—stories of disaster, health, and the ties that bind people to their environments. I trace the stories of responders and survivors, listening closely to how they navigate the chaos and repair left in the wake of environmental rupture.” She has done so as a nurse in Australia, Azerbaijan, Jordan, Malaysia, Uganda, and Ukraine, followed by research in South Africa and Europe. Physical care and storytelling were never far from mental health.

A major part of her practical experience was dealing with systemic sexism, which debilitates one’s mental health, despite the team being united in trying to save lives and prevent further injuries to patients. Healthcare, especially in disasters including conflicts, remains heavily male-dominated. Nurses are primarily women who are then subject to overt and subtle discrimination on the basis of being female.

“Women’s professional abilities are often relegated to the background,” explains Emily. “Comments about hair and lipstick, as well as sexual jokes, remain frequent topics of workplace conversation.” Yet she had to focus on dealing with each patient. Self-care meant protecting herself physically from possible injury or contamination from a patient’s body fluids, while also having to avoid physical harassment, work around the verbal harassment, and do more than men to prove her competence.

These mental health impacts are not easy to navigate, especially since physical health impacts are never too far from daily experiences. Men rarely understand hygiene requirements for menstruating when working, plus standard equipment was infrequently designed for women’s bodies, typically presuming a body shape and size based on men. Emily became motivated to seek deeper knowledge and apply it to improve practice.

For her Ph.D., “I used ethnographic and arts-based methods to examine how people lived through and after South Africa’s 2022 KwaZulu-Natal floods. I was particularly interested in the stories people told about disaster, how floods disrupted and reshaped social worlds, and the forms of repair through which people continued living with what had been lost or broken. I also considered how these experiences shaped health, which by definition must include mental health, even though this is often neglected.”

One of Emily’s key recommendations is to listen more closely to how trauma nurses and disaster responders describe the psychological impacts of their work. These accounts can reveal pressures that may otherwise go unnoticed and help us understand what enables people to remain in these roles over time.

Ethics involving mental health

Despite winning multiple awards, including being pre-selected for Global Australian of the Year in 2023, Emily’s focus is on the people she helps—those affected by disasters, including conflict and violence, her colleagues, and also herself. She explains, “The ethics of care is fundamental to what I do in practice and in research. This relates to data collection and data use, as well as to physical treatments in disaster medicine. But also how our mental health is affected when being treated and when treating, when being a ‘subject’ of research and when researching.”

In essence, Emily aims to examine, understand, and improve how people stay mentally healthy during medical situations involving physical trauma, which, in turn, links to psychological trauma. It is about the first rule of first aid, including mental health first aid: help others, but do not place yourself or others in danger to do so. Emily’s work will help us all by reducing these dangers to physical health, mental health, and their interconnections.
